newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan firms' profits on growth trend - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Japan firms' profits on growth trend - analysts.

text.p: Japanese corporate profits are expected to enjoy steady growth this business year and the trend could continue for at least two more years, analysts said on Tuesday.

The expected robust growth in profits was proof that the nation's economy was on a slow but steady recovery path, a trend likely to be confirmed in the Japanese central bank's key corporate "tankan" survey of business sentiment due out later this month.

According to reports by major Japanese research institutes, companies are likely to post eight to 12 percent rises in their total parent current profits in the year to next March, after a rise of around 10 to 13 percent the year before.

"Current profits (at major Japanese firms) marked the third straight year of increase in 1996/97. Given our profit growth estimates for 1997/98 and 1998/99, it would be a long-running rising trend, which would last for five years," Daiwa Institute of Research said in its report issued on Tuesday.

By Tuesday, a total 14 research institutes had unveiled their corporate profit outlooks for 1997/98, in which they forecast a total current profit growth of between 7.8 percent and 12.2 percent. They saw a profit growth between 6.0 percent and 11.7 percent for the following year.
In the just-ended year, most institutions saw a parent current profit growth of between 10.0 percent to 13.1 percent. The figures do not include profits of financial institutions.
"It would be the third time after World War Two for Japan to see five successive years of corporate profit growth," Nikko Research Centre said in its report.

Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities and Economics said that Japanese companies would see record combined group profits in 1997/98 because of the fast expansion of group profits at car and electric appliance makers.
Those companies aggressively shifted their production overseas to cope with the strong yen in the early 1990s.
All research institutes said that a large profit growth in the manufacturing sector, helped by a weaker yen and active exports, led overall profit growth in 1996/97.

The car industry and the electric appliance and precision machinery sector, both of which were competitive in the global market, contributed the most to the boost in overall profits in 1996/97, a research division of Nomura Securities Co Ltd said.

In 1997/98, the electric appliance and precision machinery sector and the machinery industry will continue helping boost profits, but the car industry's contribution is expected to lessen, Nomura said.
"After 1997/98, electronics will become a major player to lead overall corporate earnings growth," Daiwa said, adding that the semiconductor market would hit bottom after 1997/98.
The information and telecommunications business is expected to sharply expand after 1997/98 backed by increasing demand for digital and communication equipment, Daiwa said.
The demand would not only help the electronics sector, but benefit companies like semiconductor material producers, game software makers and information service providers, Daiwa said.
About two thirds of current profit growth in 1998/99 would be related to information and digitisation, Daiwa said.

The positive impact of a weak yen was expected to disappear by 1998/99 but selective investment and cost-cutting efforts, as well as accelerated demand for high-tech products and services, will help Japanese companies boost their profits in 1998/99, Nikko said.
